title: Night Trap: The Video Game Failure that Changed the Industry
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the 1992 full-motion video game Night Trap, prompted by a listener request after the Netflix documentary series High Score. They trace its roots in Tamara de Lempicka-inspired immersive theater (Sleep No More style), its origins at Axlon/Control Vision as a Nolan Bushnell-linked project, the Hasbro-driven shift from ninjas to vampire-like "Augurs" over reproducible-violence concerns, casting of Dana Plato, the costly shoot, and the 1992 Sega CD release. The episode covers the Lieberman and Herb Kohl hearings that helped spur creation of the ESRB, the game's later revival via a 2014 Kickstarter that fell short, a 2016 smartphone version by Tyler Hogel, and a closing listener email about speed reading.

segments.title: Opening and listener request
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a listener request about Night Trap, mention the Netflix documentary series High Score, and preview the game's significance in the video game ratings debate.

segments.title: Sleep No More inspiration and game concept
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Tamara play, a multi-room immersive piece that inspired Sleep No More, and how it inspired Night Trap's concept of switching between security camera views while missing action elsewhere.

segments.title: Control Vision, VHS technology and Dragon's Lair
segments.summary: Night Trap was built on the Control Vision platform at Axlon, using VHS-based full motion video that allowed quick switching between views via interlacing. The team was also inspired by Dragon's Lair, though Night Trap let players control the action rather than just react.

segments.title: From ninjas to Augurs: Hasbro's content restrictions
segments.summary: The original ninja concept was rejected by Hasbro over reproducible violence concerns, leading to vampires and then to the lumbering Augurs who drain blood with a tool. Focus group feedback suggested an adult audience, and the hosts discuss Hasbro's teen market goals.

segments.title: Casting, shoot, and Dana Plato
segments.summary: The game was shot on a Culver City sound stage with a roughly 250-page script and many branching outcomes. Dana Plato was cast as the anchor Kelly. The hosts discuss Plato's later death, the cartoonish violence, and cinematographer Don Burgess.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the Hasbro cliffhanger is resolved.

segments.title: Hasbro drops the game, Digital Pictures and Sega CD
segments.summary: Hasbro dropped the game as CD-ROM technology rose. Designers bought the rights and founded Digital Pictures. Sega then approached them for a Sega CD release in 1992, but the game was not very playable and its footage looked dated.

segments.title: Senate hearings, ESRB, and controversy
segments.summary: Senators Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl targeted Night Trap and Mortal Kombat, which spurred creation of the industry self-imposed ESRB rating system. The hosts argue the game was unfairly criticized since players stop the violence rather than commit it.

segments.title: Revival: Kickstarter, Tyler Hogel smartphone version, and gameplay
segments.summary: A 2014 Kickstarter to revive Night Trap failed to reach its goal. In 2016 Tyler Hogel created a smartphone version using original footage, later rated T. The hosts describe the gameplay problems of the color-code traps and branching scenes.

segments.title: Mortal Kombat movie and closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts briefly discuss the new Mortal Kombat movie on HBO Max and wrap up the Night Trap discussion.

segments.title: Listener mail: speed reading trauma
segments.summary: Listener Kate Ellis Jensen recalls elementary school speed reading drills with a transparency on an overhead projector, and the hosts respond.
